about: Rockhound Scout field list: which FORMATIONS produce which materials, by state. Not a list of spots. 'high' = documented producer; 'possible' = may contain it. Rows marked authoritative (JT's field knowledge) override the AI; researched rows can only raise the AI's rating. Patterns are case-insensitive text patterns; | means 'or'. Optional 'areas' = [[lat, lon, miles], ...] limits a row to searches near those places. 'review' marks rows that need a stronger source before launch.
generalNote: Public land rules (most BLM land): reasonable personal amounts of rocks, minerals and common invertebrate or plant fossils; petrified wood up to 25 lb plus 1 piece per day and 250 lb per year; no vertebrate fossils (bones, teeth, tracks); no collecting in national parks, developed recreation sites, or on mining claims without the claimholder's permission.

stateNotes.Hawaii: Hawaii is one of the most restrictive states for collecting. State rules prohibit taking sand, rocks, dead coral or other beach deposits from the shoreline (shells, driftwood and beach glass are allowed). Collecting is prohibited in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park and at Papakolea green-sand beach, and most zeolite outcrops are on private or military land. Many visitors photograph rather than collect.
stateNotes.Alaska: No rock, mineral or fossil collecting in national parks (the Kobuk jade country borders Gates of the Arctic). Alaska Native corporation land is private. Never pan or dig on an active mining claim without the claimholder's written permission; recreational panning is allowed on most open state and BLM land.
stateNotes.Nevada: Much of Nevada is BLM land open to casual collecting, but mining claims are everywhere — you can't collect on an active claim without the claimant's permission. Most turquoise mines are closed to the public.
stateNotes.Colorado: Much of the Pikes Peak crystal country is National Forest, but active mining claims are common and some areas (like Crystal Park) are largely private — never dig on a claim without permission.
stateNotes.Kansas: Nearly all of Kansas is private land — fossil hunting there needs the landowner's permission.
stateNotes.Nebraska: Most of Nebraska is private land. On Oglala National Grassland, personal rock collecting is allowed under casual-use rules; vertebrate fossils need a federal permit.
stateNotes.South Dakota: No collecting of any kind inside Badlands National Park or Wind Cave/Mount Rushmore. Buffalo Gap National Grassland allows surface collecting of minerals and common invertebrate fossils for personal use.
stateNotes.North Dakota: No collecting in Theodore Roosevelt National Park. Little Missouri National Grassland: 25 lb per day, 250 lb per year, no machinery, no vertebrate fossils.
stateNotes.Wisconsin: Collecting rocks, minerals and fossils is prohibited in Wisconsin State Parks.
stateNotes.Michigan: Collecting is prohibited at Isle Royale, Pictured Rocks and Sleeping Bear Dunes (National Park Service). Michigan limits collecting on state land to 25 lb.
stateNotes.Tennessee: Collecting is generally prohibited in Tennessee state parks, Great Smoky Mountains National Park and Big South Fork. Cherokee National Forest allows personal, non-commercial collecting in reasonable amounts.
stateNotes.North Carolina: Most gem collecting is at fee-dig mines on private land. Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests allow surface collecting in reasonable amounts — no digging.
stateNotes.South Carolina: Collecting fossils from the bottom of state waterways requires an SC DNR Hobby Diver License; significant finds must be reported.
stateNotes.Georgia: Collecting is prohibited in Georgia State Parks. Chattahoochee National Forest allows surface collecting for personal use.
stateNotes.Florida: Fossil shark and ray teeth, plants and invertebrates: no permit needed. Other vertebrate fossils on state land or in state waters need a Florida Fossil Permit ($5/year). No collecting in state parks, wildlife refuges, national parks or national forests.
stateNotes.Alabama: Get permission on private land (posting isn't required for trespass to apply). National forests allow casual collecting of rocks and common invertebrate fossils; no vertebrate fossils without a permit.
stateNotes.Mississippi: No collecting in Mississippi state parks. National forests: 25 lb per day plus one piece, 250 lb per year; vertebrate fossils need a permit.
stateNotes.West Virginia: Collecting is generally not permitted in state parks or the New River Gorge National Park; don't remove rock from Seneca Rocks.
stateNotes.Pennsylvania: Most collecting sites are road cuts or private land — get permission. The St. Clair fern beds are closed to the public.
stateNotes.Maryland: Calvert Cliffs State Park: beach collecting only; it's illegal to collect beneath the cliffs.
stateNotes.Connecticut: Connecticut state parks and forests prohibit removing rocks, minerals or fossils without a DEEP permit.
stateNotes.Massachusetts: No collecting at Cape Cod National Seashore. Quarries are private. Leave dinosaur tracks in place.
stateNotes.Vermont: No collecting in Vermont State Parks or state Natural Areas; other state land needs permission. Sluicing for gold needs a state permit.
stateNotes.New Hampshire: White Mountain National Forest mineral sites need a free one-day collecting permit.

rows.label: zeolite crystals
rows.note: Zeolites fill gas pockets in weathered basalt on the older islands (mainly Oahu and Kauai); most known outcrops are on private or military land.

rows.label: petrified wood
rows.high: chinle|shinarump|sonsela|petrified forest member|blue mesa|owl rock|painted desert member
rows.note: No collecting in Petrified Forest National Park. On BLM land: up to 25 lb plus 1 piece per day, 250 lb per year.

rows.label: thundereggs
rows.note: Many famous thunderegg beds are fee-dig ranches (e.g. Priday, Richardson's); some public sites need permits — check before digging.

rows.label: quartz crystals
rows.note: Many Ouachita crystal sites are pay-to-dig mines near Mount Ida and Jessieville — call ahead for fees.

rows.label: diamonds
rows.note: Crater of Diamonds State Park: pay a small fee and keep what you find.

rows.label: Lake Superior agates
rows.note: Agates formed in the North Shore lava flows; glaciers spread them through gravels across NE and central Minnesota.

rows.label: topaz crystals
rows.note: Topaz Mountain is a BLM rockhound area; topaz fades from amber to clear in sunlight.

rows.label: dinosaur bone (look, don't take on public land)
rows.note: Vertebrate fossils such as dinosaur bone can't be collected on federal land; only on private land with the owner's permission.

rows.label: thundereggs, agate and jasper
rows.note: Rockhound State Park (near Deming) allows collecting up to 15 lb per visitor; no collecting for resale.

rows.label: barite rose rocks
rows.note: Rose rocks occur mainly from just northeast of Lexington to north of Lake Stanley Draper, around Norman.

rows.label: nephrite jade
rows.note: Jade Cove area (Big Sur): loose jade may be collected only below mean high tide, by hand, and only what one person can carry; day use only.
rows.review: host rock not named in source; listed as possible only

rows.label: precious opal
rows.note: Virgin Valley opal: private fee-dig mines (e.g. Royal Peacock, Bonanza) surrounded by BLM land.

rows.label: trilobites
rows.review: Oak Springs trilobite area is BLM shale; formation name (Pioche Shale) not confirmed by source

rows.label: star garnets
rows.note: Emerald Creek star garnet area (Idaho Panhandle National Forests): advance tickets required through recreation.gov.
rows.review: source rock not named in source; possible only

rows.label: sapphires
rows.note: Montana sapphires: fee digs on the Missouri River bars near Helena (e.g. Spokane Bar) and at Gem Mountain on Rock Creek, where you buy and wash gravel.

rows.label: Montana moss agates
rows.note: Montana moss agates are found along the Yellowstone River and its tributaries; best at low water (early spring, late fall). A Montana Conservation License is needed for most state land, including fishing access sites.

rows.label: turritella (Elimia) agate
rows.review: forum source; confirm with a survey publication before launch

rows.label: fossil fish (look, don't take on public land)
rows.note: Fossil fish: no collecting at Fossil Butte National Monument; private quarries near Kemmerer offer fee digs. Vertebrate fossils can't be collected on federal land.

rows.label: petrified wood
rows.note: Ginkgo Petrified Forest State Park (Vantage) is for viewing; check state park rules before collecting anything.
rows.review: source names only the Columbia basalt group; listed as possible

rows.label: Eocene leaf and insect fossils
rows.note: Stonerose Interpretive Center (Republic): dig for your own fossils and take some home, under the center's rules.
rows.review: formation name (Klondike Mountain Fm) not in source

rows.label: almandine garnet
rows.note: Wrangell Garnet Ledge is privately owned; ask locally about permission.

rows.label: Cretaceous chalk fossils (oysters, giant clams, shark teeth)
rows.note: Western Kansas chalk is almost all private land (Monument Rocks and Castle Rock are private property open to visitors) — get the landowner's permission before collecting; bones of swimming reptiles and fish are best left to museums.
rows.review: carlile/graneros/dakota as 'possible' is my addition, not from the source

rows.label: Pennsylvanian–Permian fossils (crinoids, brachiopods, fusulinids)
rows.note: Eastern Kansas limestones and shales; road cuts are the classic exposures. Private land needs the owner's permission.
rows.review: group names in 'possible' are mine (standard Kansas group names); the source says eastern-Kansas Pennsylvanian/Permian rocks generally

rows.label: blue chalcedony (state gem), Fairburn and prairie agates
rows.note: Oglala National Grassland: personal rock and mineral collecting allowed under casual-use rules, no mechanized tools; vertebrate fossils need a federal permit.

rows.label: petrified wood
rows.note: Mostly small pieces in Ogallala gravels, Pine Ridge drainages and Platte River gravels.

rows.label: Fairburn and prairie agates
rows.note: Agate beds between Fairburn and Scenic, along French Creek and the Cheyenne River. Buffalo Gap National Grassland allows surface collecting of minerals and common invertebrate fossils for personal use; no collecting at all inside Badlands National Park.

rows.label: rose quartz and pegmatite minerals (beryl, tourmaline, garnet)
rows.note: Keystone–Custer pegmatite district; many old mines are on private claims — ask first.

rows.label: placer gold
rows.note: Fine gold in northern Hills creeks such as Whitewood and Deadwood Creeks; lode gold and active claims are off-limits.

rows.label: petrified wood
rows.note: Little Missouri National Grassland: casual collecting, 25 lb per day and 250 lb per year, no machinery, no vertebrate fossils. Theodore Roosevelt National Park: no collecting of anything.

rows.label: Knife River flint
rows.note: Never found in its original bed; pieces turn up on Knife River and Spring Creek terraces in Dunn, Mercer and Oliver counties and in gravels near Bismarck–Mandan. The Knife River Indian Villages and quarry sites are protected.
rows.review: sources disagree on the parent unit (ND Geological Survey: Golden Valley Fm, Camels Butte Mbr; rockhounding.org: Bullion Creek) — listed both as possible

rows.label: geodes and crystal pockets (calcite, galena, druzy quartz)
rows.note: Southwest Wisconsin lead-zinc country (Grant County bluffs, Platteville, Mineral Point). Collecting is prohibited in Wisconsin State Parks.

rows.label: Ordovician and Silurian fossils (brachiopods, trilobites, corals)
rows.note: Collecting is prohibited in Wisconsin State Parks.
rows.review: source is a list of fossil-bearing units, not a ranking; all set to possible

rows.label: Petoskey stones (fossil coral)
rows.note: Michigan limits collecting on state land to 25 lb; no collecting at Sleeping Bear Dunes (National Park Service).
rows.review: 'possible' Traverse-area unit names are mine; source names Gravel Point Fm / Traverse Group

rows.label: Lake Superior agates
rows.note: Upper Peninsula beaches and gravels. No collecting at Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore or Isle Royale National Park.

rows.label: native copper, greenstone (chlorastrolite) and datolite
rows.note: Keweenaw mine dumps and beaches. Mine dump ownership varies — don't assume an unposted dump is open. Collecting is prohibited on Isle Royale.

rows.label: geodes
rows.note: South-central Indiana road cuts and creek beds (around Bloomington–Bedford).
rows.review: 'possible' units are neighboring units, not named as geode-bearing in the source

rows.note: Southwest Ohio around Cincinnati, Dayton and Oxford; road cuts and creek beds. Ohio's state symbol fossil, Isotelus, comes from these rocks.

rows.label: Flint Ridge flint (Vanport)
rows.note: Flint Ridge (Licking and Muskingum counties). Flint Ridge State Memorial is a protected historic site — collect only where allowed.

rows.label: geodes
rows.note: East: Estill, Lee and Powell counties (Irvine, Red River Gorge creek bottoms). West: Breckinridge County (Rough River). Red River Gorge is in Daniel Boone National Forest — surface collecting only.

rows.label: Kentucky agate (state rock)
rows.note: Found around Irvine in parts of Estill, Powell, Jackson, Menifee, Madison and Lee counties — mostly in creek beds.
rows.review: host unit (Borden Fm / Renfro Mbr) from a mindat locality name, not a survey statement

rows.label: Ordovician fossils (brachiopods, bryozoans, trilobites)
rows.high: kope|fairview|grant lake|miamitown|bellevue|corryville|mount auburn|arnheim|waynesville|liberty|whitewater|drakes|dillsboro|saluda|cincinnati|richmond group|maysville group|eden group|clays ferry
rows.note: Northern Kentucky around Cincinnati and the Bluegrass road cuts.
rows.review: Lexington Limestone units in 'possible' are mine

rows.label: geodes
rows.note: Cannon County around Woodbury, and the Upper Cumberland belt (Fentress, Overton, Clay, White counties). Most land is private; collecting is generally prohibited in Tennessee state parks.
rows.review: source says 'Mississippian limestone' without naming units — names are mine

rows.label: agate (Paint Rock, Horse Mountain)
rows.note: Paint Rock agate: Cumberland Plateau, Sequatchie County (Mississippian limestone and chert). Horse Mountain agate: Hermitage Formation east of Shelbyville. Ask permission — mostly private land.

rows.label: fossils (Ordovician brachiopods, crinoids, corals; Devonian silicified fossils)
rows.note: Central Tennessee road cuts around Nashville; silicified Devonian fossils on the western Highland Rim. No collecting in Great Smoky Mountains NP or Big South Fork.
rows.review: 'possible' unit names are mine

rows.label: rubies and sapphires
rows.note: Cowee Valley near Franklin (Macon County) — almost all collecting is at fee-dig mines on private land.

rows.label: emerald, hiddenite and pegmatite gems (aquamarine, garnet, smoky quartz)
rows.note: Hiddenite (Alexander County): Emerald Hollow Mine is a fee dig open to the public. Spruce Pine: pegmatite district; Pisgah National Forest allows surface collecting only.

rows.label: megalodon and other shark teeth
rows.note: Aurora: the Aurora Fossil Museum's Fossil Park lets visitors dig in mine tailings and keep what they find.

rows.label: shark teeth and megalodon teeth
rows.note: Edisto Beach after storms; black-water rivers (Cooper, Edisto, Stono). Collecting from the bottom of state waterways needs an SC DNR Hobby Diver License.
rows.review: source says 'Eocene–Miocene Coastal Plain formations' — unit names are mine

rows.label: amethyst
rows.note: Pegmatite dikes near Due West (Abbeville County) — private land.

rows.label: placer gold
rows.note: Carolina Gold Belt creeks in Lancaster, York, Cherokee and Chesterfield counties (Kings Creek, Thicketty Creek).

rows.label: staurolite (fairy crosses)
rows.note: Fannin and Gilmer counties: weathers out of mica schist as creek float. Chattahoochee National Forest allows surface collecting for personal use.

rows.label: amethyst and quartz crystals
rows.note: Jackson's Crossroads (Wilkes County, private — check current access); Graves Mountain (Lincoln County, lazulite, rutile, kyanite) is private and open only on scheduled dig days.

rows.label: placer gold
rows.note: Dahlonega district (Chestatee and Etowah rivers, Yahoola Creek); pan at public access points. Collecting is prohibited in Georgia State Parks.

rows.label: shark teeth and megalodon teeth
rows.note: Fossil shark and ray teeth, plants and invertebrates need no permit. Other vertebrate fossils (bones, other teeth) on state land or in state waters need a $5/year Florida Fossil Permit. No collecting in state parks, wildlife refuges, national parks or national forests.
rows.review: unit names (Peace River, Bone Valley, Hawthorn) are mine; the source covers the permit rules only

rows.label: geodes
rows.note: North Alabama, mainly DeKalb and Jackson counties.

rows.label: Pennsylvanian plant fossils (ferns, Calamites)
rows.note: Bankhead National Forest: casual collecting of rocks and common invertebrate and plant fossils allowed; no digging or machinery.
rows.review: source says 'Pennsylvanian sandstone and shale' — Pottsville name is mine

rows.label: Cretaceous chalk shark teeth
rows.note: West-central Alabama chalk gullies (the 'Black Belt'). Mostly private land — get permission; bones of mosasaurs and turtles are best reported to a museum.
rows.review: Mooreville Chalk as 'high' is from club trip reports, not the Wikipedia source

rows.label: petrified wood (state stone)
rows.note: Red Creek cuts through the Hattiesburg and Pascagoula formations. Bienville National Forest: 25 lb per day plus one piece, 250 lb per year. No collecting in Mississippi state parks.
rows.review: catahoula/forest hill/citronelle as possible are mine

rows.label: shark teeth
rows.note: Eocene and Oligocene marine clays and creek gravels.

rows.label: petrified palmwood (state fossil)
rows.note: Central Louisiana road cuts (e.g. Highway 84 between Jena and Vidalia), creek banks and construction gravel.

rows.label: agate, jasper and chert in river gravels
rows.note: Mississippi and Red River gravel bars — material carried from far upriver, including Lake Superior agates.

rows.label: staurolite (fairy stones)
rows.note: Fairy Stone State Park (Patrick County): a small number may be taken for personal use from the park area left of the Fairy Stone Pitstop on Route 57; no commercial digging.

rows.label: Pennsylvanian plant fossils (fern impressions, coal balls)
rows.note: Shale above coal seams. Coal and mine areas need written permission from the owner or operator.
rows.review: group names are mine; source says 'Pennsylvanian coal measures'

rows.label: marine fossils (brachiopods, crinoids, horn corals)
rows.note: Devonian and Mississippian limestones and shales. Monongahela National Forest allows surface collecting of common invertebrate fossils for personal use. No collecting in the New River Gorge National Park portion.
rows.review: unit names are mine except Greenbrier

rows.label: Devonian fossils (brachiopods, corals, trilobites)
rows.note: Central Pennsylvania road cuts and borrow pits. Swatara State Park's Suedberg site and the Montour Preserve fossil pit are known public spots — check current rules.
rows.review: 'possible' units are mine

rows.label: Pennsylvanian fern and plant fossils
rows.note: Anthracite region (Schuylkill County). The famous St. Clair fern beds are fenced and closed to the public — some clubs get permission.
rows.review: 'possible' units are mine

rows.label: Cretaceous shark teeth, belemnites and oysters (Big Brook)
rows.note: Big Brook (Colts Neck/Marlboro): township rules posted at the 88 Hillsdale Road lot — five fossils per person per day, shovel blade up to 6 inches, groups of 15+ need a permit.
rows.review: unit names are mine (standard Monmouth County units); source names none

rows.label: fluorescent minerals (Franklin–Sterling Hill)
rows.note: Collect at the Buckwheat Dump behind the Franklin Mineral Museum for a small admission and per-pound fee.

rows.label: belemnites (state fossil) and Cretaceous fossils
rows.note: Dredge spoil piles on the north side of the Chesapeake & Delaware Canal, west of St. Georges.
rows.review: 'possible' units are mine

rows.label: Miocene shark teeth and shells (Calvert Cliffs)
rows.note: Calvert Cliffs State Park: collect on the open beach at the end of the red trail (about 1.8 miles); it's illegal to collect beneath the cliffs, and climbing them is prohibited.
rows.review: unit names from general knowledge (state page says Miocene only)

rows.label: almandine garnet (state mineral)
rows.note: Western highlands schist around Roxbury and Housatonic River gravels. CT state parks and forests prohibit removing rocks and minerals without a DEEP permit.

rows.label: pegmatite minerals (black tourmaline, beryl)
rows.note: Portland and Haddam pegmatites (Middlesex County) — old quarries are mostly private.

rows.label: traprock minerals (prehnite, zeolites)
rows.note: Meriden area basalt quarries (private). No collecting at Sleeping Giant State Park.

rows.label: cumberlandite (state rock)
rows.note: Source is Iron Mine Hill in Cumberland; pieces are spread through glacial deposits of the Narragansett Bay area.

rows.label: traprock minerals (prehnite, babingtonite, datolite)
rows.note: Connecticut Valley basalt quarries (e.g. Lane Quarry, Westfield) are private — permission required.

rows.label: dinosaur tracks (look, don't take)
rows.note: Removing tracks from known protected sites is illegal; leave loose track slabs in place.

rows.label: garnet, kyanite and staurolite
rows.note: Gassetts road cut on Route 103 (Williams River) and Windham County brooks. Landowner permission required; no collecting in Vermont State Parks or Natural Areas.

rows.label: placer gold
rows.note: Broad Brook (Plymouth), Mad River, Rock River, Lamoille and Missisquoi rivers. Hand panning differs from sluicing — sluice boxes need a state permit.

rows.label: Ordovician fossils (trilobites, brachiopods, gastropods)

rows.note: Lake Champlain shoreline near Chimney Point. The Chazy Reef at Isle La Motte is a protected preserve.
rows.review: unit names other than Crown Point are mine

rows.label: smoky quartz, microcline and topaz (Conway granite)
rows.note: Moat Mountain Mineral Site (White Mountain National Forest): a free one-day collecting permit from the trailhead is required.

rows.label: tourmaline, apatite and pegmatite minerals
rows.note: Mount Apatite Park (Auburn): amateurs may search the old mine tailings for apatite, tourmaline and quartz under the city's posted rules.
